claims.text: A CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy can undergo a controlled ductile–brittle–ductile transition across the temper-embrittlement temperature range.
The CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy can avoid the dramatic ductility loss found in conventional alloys during that transition.
Arc melting and homogenization produce a uniform elemental distribution in the proposed CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy.
The proposed as-homogenized alloy has a moderate grain size of approximately 10–50 µm.
CoCrFeMnNi is an HEA that commonly forms an FCC solid solution.
Near-equiatomic multicomponent HEAs possess high configurational entropy.
Slight variations in Mn or Ni content can be used to control the proposed transition.
Heat treatments in the 400–600 °C range are associated with temper embrittlement in steels.
Changing HEA composition or annealing temperature can cause or tune phase decomposition.
High configurational entropy limits grain-boundary segregation in CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs.
The CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA retains a stable solid-solution microstructure under the proposed 400–600 °C treatment.
The stable solid-solution microstructure suppresses typical embrittling phases.
Multicomponent alloy design curbs the formation of embrittling phases.
Multicomponent alloy design curbs grain-boundary segregation.
Suppressing embrittling phases and grain-boundary segregation reduces local stress concentrations and preserves ductility.
The proposed HEA will not exhibit a sharp drop in ductility between 400 and 600 °C.
Conventional steels commonly undergo a sudden loss of toughness and ductility because of temper embrittlement at 400–600 °C.
Large composition changes or different annealing temperatures may modify the alloy's phases and resulting behavior.
Grain-size control is required for the proposed behavior.
The optimal compositional window for the proposed transition has not been determined.

contradictions.description: A ductile–brittle–ductile transition implies an intervening brittle regime or measurable ductility reduction, whereas the predicted outcome describes no sharp ductility drop and calls that stable behavior a ductile–brittle–ductile transition. The falsification rule likewise contrasts embrittlement with the proposed transition without defining how a brittle stage can occur without significant ductility loss.
